study_guide.title: Where the Storm Is Born

pages.text: Cane the Weather Dog stood on the sunny beach and looked far, far out at the water. "Do you know where the biggest storms in the world are born?" he asked. "Not on land. Way out here — over the warm ocean." Far away, near the middle of the Earth, the ocean is warm all year. This warm part is called the tropics. When the water gets to about 80 degrees — as warm as a bathtub — it is ready to make a storm.
pages.ask: Put your hand out flat like the ocean. Can you feel warm sunshine on it?

pages.text: "Here is the secret," said Cane. "When the sun warms the ocean, tiny bits of water float up into the sky. That is called evaporating. Now the air is warm and full of water. We call it moist air." The warm, moist air floated up, up, up. It made tall clouds. And those clouds gave the storm its power. "Warm, moist air is the storm's fuel," said Cane. "Fuel is what keeps something going — like food gives YOU energy to run and play."
pages.ask: What gives you energy to run? (Food!) What gives a hurricane energy? (Warm, moist air!)

pages.text: To build a hurricane, nature needs three things to come together, like a recipe: 1. Warm ocean water. 2. Lots of moist air. 3. Winds that come together and start it spinning.

When all three are ready, the little storm begins to spin. First it is a small tropical storm. If it keeps drinking up warm, moist air, it grows bigger and stronger — until it becomes a hurricane. "But here is the best part," said Cane, wagging his tail. "A hurricane is born far, far away. It takes days to travel across the ocean. That gives us lots of time to get our family ready. We are never surprised." Cane smiled at the sea. "The ocean makes the storm. And smart scientists watch the whole time — so families stay safe. You're learning to be one of those weather watchers!"
pages.ask: Can you spin in a slow circle like a growing storm?

study_guide.rule: Hurricanes are born over warm ocean water — the warm water is their fuel!
